headline: With a distinct translateX per element and nobody hand-optimizing, next-yak's automatic css-var split holds flat while the runtime hashers regenerate a class per element: `goober` renders 9.7× slower and its client mount blows out to 1270 ms.

microbench.why: next-yak compiles the dynamic value into a static class plus a CSS custom property, so `next-yak-css-9.7` writes one class and a `--var` per element at 0.601 ms/1k, tying `vanilla` (0.604); `StyleX` handles it as a static class with an inline value at 0.859. The naive pattern punishes the hashers, which re-derive a class for every distinct value: `styled-components`'s `generateAndInjectStyles` returns to the hot path at 4.75 ms/1k, `panda`'s serializer 3.54, `goober`'s compile-and-hash 5.83, 9.7× the css-prop path.

autocannon.why: Serving distinct values under load, the css-var split holds 1276 req/s next to `vanilla` (1213); the styled perf runtime 713. The hashers collapse as each request regenerates every class, `goober` 158 req/s, `styled-components` 196, `panda` 239.

attribution.why: The css-var split renders in 0.646 ms with a 0.111 ms library slice, under `vanilla` (0.923 ms) which sets an inline `style` per element. The styled perf runtime routes the value through the same css-var but keeps its `Yak` wrapper (0.455 ms library, 1.31 ms). The hashers pay their full pipeline per distinct value: `goober` 4.83 ms of 6.49 ms, `styled-components` 3.52 ms, `panda`'s per-element `css()` serializer 3.31 ms of component self-time.

hydrate.why: The css-var split hydrates at 47.4 ms; the styled perf runtime 51.9 ms. `goober` collapses to 1279 ms, injecting 1000 distinct classes into the sheet during hydration and forcing reflow on each, the run's worst client phase; `styled-components` 114 ms and `emotion` 97.8 ms show the same per-class inject at smaller scale.

inp.why: Re-rendering one element with a fresh value costs ~7.30-7.40 ms across the css-var and static-class lanes, a tie. The hashers re-derive and re-inject on the change, `panda` 16.8 ms, `goober` 22.7 ms.

mount.why: Cold mount of the css-var split is 62.4 ms; the styled perf runtime 67.4 ms. `goober` blows out to 1270 ms injecting 1000 distinct classes on first paint, against `emotion` 117 ms and `styled-components` 111 ms.

renderTiming.why: One recalc per lane; distinct dynamic values change the JS render and the injected-sheet size, not the browser's recalc count. `goober`'s styleMs is inflated by parsing 1000 injected rules, not by extra recalcs.

payload.why: The css-var split ships static classes plus per-element `--var` values at 5.24 kB gzipped, under `vanilla` (5.50 kB). The hashers ship a distinct class per element in the HTML and their runtime, `styled-components` 35.3 kB, `emotion` 39.1 kB, 6× the css-prop fold.

nsweep.why: Scaling distinct values to 4000 elements, the css-var split holds 2.63 ms near `vanilla` (2.74), while the styled perf runtime reaches 5.07 ms. `goober` explodes to 158 ms as its per-value compile-and-hash and sheet inject scale linearly, `styled-components` 18.7 ms.

crossCase: `dyn-translate` is the naive end of the dynamic-value trio with `dyn-fair` and `dyn-inline` below. It is what you get when nobody hand-optimizes: the hashers regenerate a class per value and blow out (`goober` 5.83 vs 0.601 ms/1k for the css-var split). `dyn-fair` gives each library its hand-written best practice and the field converges; `dyn-inline` is the pure inline-style control. next-yak's css-var split ships that optimization as a feature, so it already sits at the `dyn-fair` floor here with no manual work.
